why_use_this:
Reach for this package whenever a signal needs to move between the time domain and the frequency domain -- finding what frequencies are present in a sampled waveform, filtering via convolution, or analyzing a system's stability via the Laplace/Z-transform. Use `fft`/`ifft`/`fft_real` (the fast \( O(n\log n) \) Cooley-Tukey path) whenever your data length is a power of 2 -- pad it there first with `next_power_of_two` + `zero_pad`/`zero_pad_complex` if it isn't. Fall back to `dft`/`idft` (the naive \( O(n^2) \) path, any length at all) only when padding to a power of 2 genuinely isn't an option, or as a reference implementation to cross-check `fft` against (which is exactly how this package's own tests validate `fft`'s correctness). Every frequency-domain function works in [vani-complex](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-complex)'s `Complex` type, since a frequency-domain signal is complex-valued in general even when the original time-domain signal is real.

A running example threads through the DFT-family notes below: the 4-sample signal \(x=(1,\,0,\,-1,\,0)\) -- a discretized cosine wave completing exactly one full cycle over the 4 samples (\(x_n=\cos(\pi n/2)\)), chosen because its transform comes out to clean, small numbers.

dft.intuition: The DFT asks, for each candidate frequency, "how well does a wave AT this frequency match what I'm seeing in my signal?" -- it does this by multiplying the signal against a test wave (a complex exponential) at each frequency and summing up the result; a strong match produces a large sum, no match produces a sum near zero.
dft.example: For the running example \(x=(1,0,-1,0)\) (\(N=4\)): \(X_0 = \sum_n x_n = 1+0-1+0=0\) (no constant/DC component, makes sense -- the signal is symmetric around zero). \(X_1 = 1\cdot e^0 + 0\cdot e^{-i\pi/2} + (-1)\cdot e^{-i\pi} + 0\cdot e^{-i3\pi/2} = 1\cdot1 + 0 + (-1)(-1) + 0 = 1+1=2\). By similar computation, \(X_2=0\) and \(X_3=2\). So \(X=(0,\,2,\,0,\,2)\) -- strong response at bins 1 and 3, exactly where you'd expect: this signal IS a pure cosine completing one cycle over the 4 samples, i.e. frequency bin 1 (and its mirror-image bin \(N-1=3\), the "negative frequency" component every real signal's spectrum has).
dft.why: Notice bins 1 and 3 got EQUAL, nonzero values while bins 0 and 2 came out exactly zero -- this is the DFT correctly identifying "this signal is a pure tone at frequency bin 1" with no other frequency content at all, exactly the property that makes the DFT useful for frequency analysis in the first place.

idft.intuition: Runs the DFT's logic backward: given how strongly each frequency is present, reconstruct the original signal by adding up that many waves at their respective frequencies and strengths.
idft.example: Recover \(x_0\) from the running example's spectrum \(X=(0,2,0,2)\): \(x_0 = \tfrac14(X_0+X_1+X_2+X_3) = \tfrac14(0+2+0+2)=\tfrac44=1\) -- matching the original \(x_0=1\). Recover \(x_1\): \(x_1=\tfrac14(X_0 + X_1e^{i\pi/2} + X_2e^{i\pi} + X_3e^{i3\pi/2}) = \tfrac14(0 + 2i + 0 + 2(-i)) = \tfrac14(2i-2i)=\tfrac04=0\) -- matching the original \(x_1=0\).
idft.why: The \(1/N\) normalization is what makes `idft` a true inverse rather than just a differently-signed DFT -- without it, running `dft` then `idft` would scale the signal up by a factor of \(N\) instead of recovering it exactly.

fft.intuition: Splits the problem in half, recursively: a length-\(N\) DFT can be built from two length-\(N/2\) DFTs (one over the even-indexed samples, one over the odd-indexed ones), combined with a small correction factor per output bin -- and since each half can itself be split again, the total work drops from \(O(N^2)\) all the way to \(O(N\log N)\).
fft.formula: Computes the same result as `dft`, via recursively splitting into even/odd-indexed sub-DFTs and combining with twiddle factors \(e^{-2\pi ik/N}\). Requires \(N\) to be a power of 2.
fft.example: For the running example \(x=(1,0,-1,0)\): split into evens \(e=(x_0,x_2)=(1,-1)\) and odds \(o=(x_1,x_3)=(0,0)\). The 2-point DFT of \(e\) is \(E=(E_0,E_1)=(1+(-1),\ 1-(-1))=(0,\,2)\). The 2-point DFT of \(o\) is trivially \(O=(0,0)\) (all zeros in, all zeros out). Combine using \(X_k = E_{k\bmod2} + e^{-2\pi ik/4}\,O_{k\bmod2}\): since every \(O\) term is zero, the twiddle factors don't even matter this time -- \(X_0=E_0+O_0=0\), \(X_1=E_1+O_1=2\), \(X_2=E_0+O_0=0\), \(X_3=E_1+O_1=2\). Result \((0,2,0,2)\) -- matching `dft`'s answer on the same input exactly, as it must.
fft.why: This particular example's odd half happening to be all-zero is a coincidence of this specific signal, not a general property -- for a signal where BOTH halves have real content, the twiddle factors \(e^{-2\pi ik/N}\) genuinely rotate the odd half's contribution before adding it to the even half's, which is the actual mechanism that makes the recursive combination correct in general.

ifft.intuition: The same recursive even/odd split as `fft`, run for the inverse direction -- flip the twiddle factors' sign and normalize by \(1/N\) at the end, same relationship `idft` has to `dft`.
ifft.formula: Same recursive structure as `fft`, twiddle factors \(e^{+2\pi ik/N}\), final \(1/N\) scaling.
ifft.example: Running `ifft` on the running example's spectrum \(X=(0,2,0,2)\) recovers \(x=(1,0,-1,0)\) -- the same recovery `idft`'s example already verified by hand, just reached via the faster recursive algorithm instead of the direct summation.
ifft.why: For any power-of-2 length, `ifft` and `idft` are mathematically IDENTICAL functions computed two different ways -- reach for `ifft` purely for speed on longer signals, never because it computes something different.

fft_real.intuition: A convenience wrapper: your samples are ordinary real numbers, but `fft` internally works with `Complex` values -- rather than making you manually wrap each sample as `Complex{re: x, im: 0}` yourself, this does it for you.
fft_real.formula: `fft` applied to real-valued input, each sample treated as `Complex{re: x_n, im: 0.0}`.
fft_real.example: Calling `fft_real` on the plain `Vec<f64>` \((1,0,-1,0)\) gives exactly the same spectrum \((0,2,0,2)\) as calling `fft` on the `Complex`-wrapped version of the same values -- purely a convenience, no different math underneath.
fft_real.why: This implementation returns the FULL \(N\)-length complex spectrum rather than exploiting the fact that a real signal's spectrum is conjugate-symmetric (\(X_{N-k}=\overline{X_k}\), visible directly in the running example: \(X_1=2\) and \(X_3=2\) are equal here because both are real, a special case of that general symmetry) -- a more specialized real-FFT implementation could compute only the first half and derive the rest for free, but this one doesn't take that shortcut.

dft_magnitude.intuition: A complex spectrum value \(X_k\) carries two pieces of information: how STRONG that frequency is, and what PHASE (timing offset) it has. Magnitude keeps only the strength, discarding the phase -- the number you'd actually plot on a typical "frequency spectrum" graph.
dft_magnitude.example: For the running example's spectrum \(X=(0,2,0,2)\), every value is already purely real (zero imaginary part), so the magnitude is just the absolute value: \(|X_0|=0\), \(|X_1|=2\), \(|X_2|=0\), \(|X_3|=2\) -- unchanged from the raw values in this particular case, though for a spectrum with genuine imaginary parts, magnitude would combine both real and imaginary contributions via the square root.
dft_magnitude.why: This is exactly [vani-complex](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-complex)'s `complex_abs` applied to every bin -- a spectrum's magnitude and a complex number's modulus are the same mathematical operation, just applied across a whole array.

dft_power.intuition: Squaring the magnitude is proportional to ENERGY at that frequency (physically, power often scales with amplitude squared) and conveniently skips the square root `dft_magnitude` needs -- cheaper to compute, and the natural quantity when you care about relative energy rather than relative amplitude.
dft_power.example: For the running example: power at bin 1 is \(2^2=4\), same at bin 3, and \(0\) at bins 0 and 2 -- the same relative picture as `dft_magnitude`'s answer, just each value squared.
dft_power.why: Because squaring exaggerates differences (a magnitude twice as large becomes a power four times as large), the power spectrum makes a dominant frequency stand out even more clearly against background noise than the magnitude spectrum does -- part of why "power spectral density" rather than plain magnitude is the standard tool in signal-processing practice.

fft_freq.intuition: A bin INDEX by itself doesn't tell you the actual frequency in Hz -- that depends on how fast you sampled. This function does that conversion, and also handles a subtlety: bins past the halfway point represent NEGATIVE frequencies (a standard FFT output quirk, not a bug), wrapped around to the end of the array instead of listed as negative numbers directly in the bin ordering.
fft_freq.example: For the running example (\(N=4\)) with a sample rate of 4 Hz: bin 0 is \(0\) Hz (DC). Bin 1 is \(1\times4/4=1\) Hz. Bin 2 is \(2\times4/4=2\) Hz (the Nyquist frequency, the highest frequency this sample rate can represent at all). Bin 3, since \(3\ge N/2=2\), is \((3-4)\times4/4=-1\) Hz -- the "negative frequency" mirror of bin 1's \(+1\) Hz. This lines up exactly with the running example's spectrum: the strong response was at bins 1 and 3, i.e. at \(+1\) Hz and \(-1\) Hz -- precisely the positive and negative frequency components a REAL-valued 1 Hz cosine wave should show up as.
fft_freq.why: Understanding this mapping is essential for reading an FFT's output correctly -- without it, you might mistake the second half of the bin array for higher positive frequencies, when they're actually the mirror-image negative frequencies of a real signal's inherently symmetric spectrum.

conv_linear.intuition: Convolution slides one signal across another, and at each relative position, multiplies the overlapping samples together and adds them up -- like sliding a stencil across a strip of paper and, at each position, summing up how much the stencil's pattern lines up with what's underneath it.
conv_linear.example: Convolve \(a=(1,2)\) with \(b=(1,1)\): \(c_0 = a_0b_0 = 1\times1=1\). \(c_1 = a_0b_1+a_1b_0 = 1\times1+2\times1=3\). \(c_2=a_1b_1=2\times1=2\). Result \(c=(1,3,2)\), length \(2+2-1=3\). Sanity check via polynomial multiplication (convolution IS polynomial coefficient multiplication): \((1+2x)(1+x) = 1+x+2x+2x^2=1+3x+2x^2\), coefficients \((1,3,2)\) -- matches exactly.
conv_linear.why: This direct double loop costs \(O(nm)\) -- fine for the modest sizes this library targets, but for VERY long signals, computing the same convolution via the DFT (multiply the two spectra pointwise, then inverse-transform, an \(O(n\log n)\) route) would be dramatically faster -- the convolution theorem `conv_circular`'s note references.

conv_circular.intuition: The same sliding-and-multiplying idea as `conv_linear`, but on a signal that WRAPS AROUND like a ring instead of growing longer -- whatever would have spilled past the end just wraps back around to the beginning.
conv_circular.example: Circularly convolve \(a=(1,2)\) with \(b=(1,1)\) (\(n=2\)): \(c_0 = a_0b_0+a_1b_{(0-1)\bmod2} = a_0b_0+a_1b_1=1\times1+2\times1=3\). \(c_1=a_0b_1+a_1b_0=1\times1+2\times1=3\). Result \((3,3)\). Compare with `conv_linear`'s result on the same inputs, \((1,3,2)\): notice \(c_0=3\) here is exactly `conv_linear`'s \(c_0+c_2=1+2=3\) -- the position-2 value that would have extended past the 2-sample ring WRAPPED AROUND and got added into position 0 instead.
conv_circular.why: This wrap-around behavior is exactly what corresponds to pointwise multiplication of two DFT spectra (the convolution theorem) -- if you multiplied `dft(a)` and `dft(b)` bin-by-bin and inverse-transformed, you'd get THIS circular result, not `conv_linear`'s growing-length result.

correlate.intuition: Convolution flips one signal before sliding it across the other; correlation does NOT -- it just slides one signal past the other directly and measures overlap at each position. This distinction matters because correlation answers a different question: "how similar are these two signals at this offset", not "what's their convolved combination."
correlate.formula: Like `conv_linear`, but without reversing either input -- \((a\star b)_\text{lag} = \sum_k a_k\,b_{k+\text{lag}}\).
correlate.example: Using \(a=(1,2)\) and \(b=(1,0)\): at zero lag, `correlate` computes \(a_0b_0+a_1b_1 = 1\times1+2\times0=1\) -- directly comparing corresponding positions. `conv_linear` on the same inputs instead computes \(c_1=a_0b_1+a_1b_0=1\times0+2\times1=2\) -- involving \(b\) read in REVERSE relative to \(a\). Same two input signals, genuinely different numbers, because one reverses and the other doesn't.
correlate.why: This no-reversal property is exactly why correlation (not convolution) is the right tool for finding where a known short pattern occurs inside a longer signal -- sliding the pattern across the signal and looking for a peak in the correlation directly answers "where does this pattern best match", without needing to pre-reverse the pattern to compensate for convolution's built-in flip.

window_hann.intuition: Analyzing a finite chunk of a signal is like listening to a song through a window that opens and shuts abruptly -- the abrupt cutoff itself introduces artificial high-frequency content that isn't really in the original signal ("spectral leakage"). A window function tapers the chunk's edges down smoothly to zero first, so there's no abrupt cutoff left to leak.
window_hann.example: For \(n=5\) (indices \(0\) to \(4\)): at the left edge, \(w_0 = 0.5(1-\cos0)=0.5(1-1)=0\). At the center, \(w_2=0.5(1-\cos\pi)=0.5(1-(-1))=0.5\times2=1\). At the right edge, \(w_4=0.5(1-\cos2\pi)=0.5(1-1)=0\). So the window shape is \((0,\ldots,1,\ldots,0)\) -- exactly zero at both ends, rising smoothly to full strength \(1\) in the middle.
window_hann.why: Tapering all the way to EXACTLY zero at both endpoints (unlike `window_hamming` below) is what gives the Hann window its particular tradeoff: very low leakage right at the edges, at the cost of a slightly wider main lobe than Hamming's compromise shape.

window_hamming.intuition: Almost the same cosine taper as `window_hann`, but deliberately NOT reaching all the way to zero at the edges -- a small discontinuity is accepted in exchange for a narrower, sharper peak in the resulting frequency spectrum.
window_hamming.example: For \(n=5\): at the edge, \(w_0=0.54-0.46\cos0=0.54-0.46=0.08\) -- NOT zero, unlike Hann's \(w_0=0\) for the same \(n\). At the center, \(w_2=0.54-0.46\cos\pi=0.54-0.46(-1)=0.54+0.46=1.0\), same peak value as Hann.
window_hamming.why: That small leftover value \(0.08\) at the edges (instead of Hann's exact \(0\)) is a deliberate, carefully-tuned tradeoff -- the 0.54/0.46 coefficients (rather than Hann's 0.5/0.5) were chosen specifically to minimize the largest side-lobe in the resulting spectrum, at the cost of not tapering fully to zero.

window_blackman.intuition: Adds a SECOND cosine term (at double the frequency of the first) to Hann's basic taper shape, giving finer control over the taper's exact profile -- specifically, pushing side-lobe leakage even lower than Hann or Hamming manage, at the cost of a wider main lobe.
window_blackman.example: For \(n=5\): at the edge, \(w_0 = 0.42-0.5\cos0+0.08\cos0 = 0.42-0.5+0.08=0.00\) -- tapers all the way to zero, like Hann. At the center, \(w_2=0.42-0.5\cos\pi+0.08\cos2\pi = 0.42+0.5+0.08=1.0\), same peak as the others.
window_blackman.why: Reach for Blackman specifically when you need to pick out a WEAK tone sitting close to a much STRONGER one in the spectrum -- its much lower side-lobe leakage means the strong tone's energy is less likely to bleed into and mask the weak one's bin, at the cost of the wider main lobe making the two tones need to be further apart in frequency to resolve as distinct peaks at all.

window_bartlett.intuition: The simplest possible taper: no cosine shaping at all, just a straight line up from zero to the peak and back down -- a triangle.
window_bartlett.formula: A linear ramp from \(0\) to \(1\) at the center and back to \(0\).
window_bartlett.example: For \(n=5\): \(w_0=0\), \(w_1=0.5\), \(w_2=1\) (center), \(w_3=0.5\), \(w_4=0\) -- straight-line interpolation between the endpoints and the peak, no curve.
window_bartlett.why: Cheaper to compute than any of the cosine-based windows (no trigonometric function calls needed at all, just linear interpolation) but with worse side-lobe suppression than Hann/Hamming/Blackman for the same window length -- a genuine speed-vs-quality tradeoff, not a strictly worse choice.

window_kaiser.intuition: Instead of a fixed taper shape, this window has a DIAL (\(\beta\)) that continuously trades main-lobe width against side-lobe suppression -- turn \(\beta\) up for less leakage at the cost of a wider peak, turn it down for the opposite. The fixed-shape windows above are each just one specific point along this same dial.
window_kaiser.formula: \[ w_i = \dfrac{I_0\!\left(\beta\sqrt{1-\left(\tfrac{2i}{n-1}-1\right)^2}\right)}{I_0(\beta)} \] where \(I_0\) is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind.
window_kaiser.example: The one easily hand-checkable special case is \(\beta=0\): the argument to \(I_0\) in the numerator becomes \(0\times(\cdot)=0\) for EVERY \(i\), regardless of position, so the numerator is \(I_0(0)\) everywhere; the denominator is also \(I_0(0)\); so \(w_i = I_0(0)/I_0(0) = 1\) for every \(i\) -- a completely flat window, identical to `window_rectangular`.
window_kaiser.why: This confirms the window family's claim of "generalizing the fixed-shape windows": at \(\beta=0\) it reduces exactly to the no-taper-at-all rectangular window, and as \(\beta\) increases from there, it smoothly grows a taper, trading away main-lobe width for side-lobe suppression the whole way up.

window_tukey.intuition: A hybrid: flat like a rectangular window in the middle (no taper needed there, since the middle isn't where the abrupt-cutoff problem lives), with the tapering only applied near the two edges, over a fraction \(\alpha\) of the window's total length.
window_tukey.formula: Flat in the middle; cosine-tapered (a fraction \(\alpha\) of a Hann-style taper) at each edge.
window_tukey.example: At \(\alpha=0\), there's no tapered region at all -- the whole window is flat, identical to `window_rectangular`. At \(\alpha=1\), the tapered region covers the ENTIRE window, leaving no flat middle -- identical to `window_hann`. At \(\alpha=0.5\) (a common middle-ground choice), the outer quarter on each side tapers like Hann while the middle half stays completely flat at \(1\).
window_tukey.why: This makes Tukey a genuine "slider" between two extremes covered by other functions in this package (`window_rectangular` and `window_hann`) -- useful when you want SOME leakage reduction from tapering but don't want to give up as much of the flat, undistorted middle section as a full Hann window would cost you.

laplace_transform_numeric.intuition: The (continuous) Laplace transform is normally an integral over an infinite time range -- not something you can compute from a finite set of samples exactly. This function does the honest, practical thing: numerically integrate (trapezoidal-style) over whatever finite, SAMPLED time range you actually give it, which approximates the transform restricted to that observed window of time.
laplace_transform_numeric.formula: \[ X(s) = \int_0^\infty x(t)\,e^{-st}\,dt \] approximated by trapezoidal summation over the given sampled \((t,x)\) points.
laplace_transform_numeric.example: With just two samples, \(t=(0,1)\) and \(x=(1,1)\) (a constant signal, sampled only briefly), and \(s=1\): the trapezoidal estimate is \(\tfrac12\big(x(0)e^{-0} + x(1)e^{-1}\big)\times(t_1-t_0) = \tfrac12(1\times1 + 1\times e^{-1})\times1 \approx \tfrac12(1+0.368) \approx 0.684\).
laplace_transform_numeric.why: Compare this to the TRUE Laplace transform of a constant signal \(x(t)=1\) integrated over ALL time, which has the well-known closed form \(1/s\) (here, \(1/1=1\)) -- the numeric estimate of \(0.684\) is noticeably different, because it only integrates over the brief \(t\in[0,1]\) window actually sampled, not the true infinite domain. More/longer samples would bring the numeric estimate closer to the closed-form answer for signals where the closed form actually converges.

z_transform_numeric.intuition: The Z-transform is the discrete-signal cousin of the Laplace transform, and it has a beautiful special property: evaluating it at points around the UNIT CIRCLE in the complex plane gives you exactly the DFT.
z_transform_numeric.example: Evaluate the running example \(x=(1,0,-1,0)\)'s Z-transform at \(z=e^{i2\pi/4}=e^{i\pi/2}=i\) (the unit-circle point corresponding to bin \(k=1\) of a length-4 DFT): \(X(i) = x_0\,i^0 + x_1\,i^{-1} + x_2\,i^{-2} + x_3\,i^{-3} = 1\times1 + 0 + (-1)\times i^{-2} + 0\). Since \(i^2=-1\), \(i^{-2}=1/(-1)=-1\), so \(X(i) = 1 + (-1)\times(-1) = 1+1=2\) -- EXACTLY matching `dft`'s \(X_1=2\) computed earlier on this same signal.
z_transform_numeric.why: This agreement isn't a coincidence for this one example -- it's the general identity this package's own tests confirm directly: the DFT is exactly the Z-transform sampled at \(N\) equally-spaced points around the unit circle, \(z_k=e^{i2\pi k/N}\).

z_transform_inverse.intuition: Runs the Z-transform backward: given samples of \(X(z)\) taken around a circle in the complex plane, reconstruct the original discrete sequence -- the discrete-signal cousin of `laplace_transform_numeric`'s continuous inverse problem, using a contour integral instead of an infinite-time integral.
z_transform_inverse.formula: A numerical contour-integral approximation evaluated on a circle of radius \(r\), recovering \(x_n\) from samples of \(X(z)\) around that circle.
z_transform_inverse.example: Feeding this function the SAME spectrum \(X=(0,2,0,2)\) the running example's `z_transform_numeric` produces (sampled on the unit circle, \(r=1\)) recovers the original \((1,0,-1,0)\) -- the same round-trip `idft` already demonstrated, just reached via the Z-transform's contour-integral machinery instead of the DFT's direct summation.
z_transform_inverse.why: Any leftover imaginary-part residue from the numerical contour integration is discarded before returning the result, since a REAL sequence's Z-transform inverse is mathematically guaranteed to be real -- any nonzero imaginary part surviving in the numeric computation is purely floating-point rounding noise, not a genuine signal component.
